```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# readr rather than datawizard::data_read(), which reads empty cells as "" and
# the codes of the cases, strata and clusters as numbers
analysts <- readr::read_csv("data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                  col_types = readr::cols(stat_type = readr::col_character()))
unions <- readr::read_csv("data/cohab_unions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                   col_types = readr::cols(caseid = readr::col_character(), stratum = readr::col_character(),
                                    psu = readr::col_character()))
score <- readr::read_csv("data/score_person_months.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
repro <- readr::read_csv("data/display_reproduction.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
menu <- readr::read_csv("data/menu_options.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

fmt <- \(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
big <- \(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
an <- \(id, col) analysts[[col]][analysts$id == id]

ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
paper <- datawizard::data_filter(unions, cycle %in% c("1995", "2006-10"), in_window, cycle == "1995" | from_2005)
model_2 <- datawizard::data_filter(repro, model == 2, equation == "marriage", term == "later")
# the outcome of each union of 1995 in the SCORE file is that of its last row
score_1995 <- score |>
  datawizard::data_filter(P95 == 1) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(MONTHNUM, n = 1, by = CASEID) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(n = n(), by = "OUTCOME")
s95 <- \(code) score_1995$n[score_1995$OUTCOME == code]
n_decisions <- dplyr::n_distinct(menu$axis)
```

This page sets out the whole exercise of the course on the cohabitation case. The [case study](index.qmd) presents the original study, the five Multi100 reanalyses, the file that the analysts received and the replications, and it is the place to start if you have not read it. Your work happens in the workspace that you downloaded and opened in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), as the [Setup page](../../setup.qmd) describes. The [browser lab](lab.qmd) is a demonstration of the same exercise in a browser tab: it fits no model before Task 3, and shows every result as the course pipeline computed it with the code of the workspace, beside that code, so it gives the same numbers; the reproduction of Task 3 runs there in full. It serves for following a demonstration and for submitting to the class chart if your machine fails; to fit a specification yourself, use the workspace. The page of your track gives the timing of each task.

---

## The claim

Five independent analysts reanalysed one claim of the original authors (OAs) in the Multi100 project [@KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion]. The claim, as the analysts received it, was the end of a sentence in the conclusions of the paper:

> "cohabitors have increasingly become less likely to progress to marriage" (p. 932)

The published result behind it is a coefficient from a discrete-time event-history model, fitted to one row for every month in which a first cohabitation could end, a person-month: **−0.683, with a standard error of 0.14**, on 54,291 person-months of women interviewed by the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) in 1995 and in 2006–2010. It compares the unions begun in 2005–2010 with those begun in 1990–1995, on the log scale of the model, and a coefficient of −0.683 means that the monthly chance that a couple of the later cohort married, rather than stayed together, was about half that of a couple of the earlier cohort. It comes from a model with interactions of race-ethnicity and period, so it is the change for non-Hispanic white women, a point that Task 3 takes up. The data are the `r big(nrow(unions))` first premarital cohabitations that the course rebuilt from five surveys of the NSFG, among them the `r big(sum(paper$cycle == "1995"))` and `r big(sum(paper$cycle == "2006-10"))` unions of the two cohorts of the paper, and the person-month file that Multi100 gave the analysts.

Your first job is to reproduce the value that Multi100 recorded for one of the analysts, from the file that the analysts received, and then to find out why it points the wrong way. Your second is to depart from the analysis of the paper deliberately, with a written reason, and to find out what that does to the estimate.

## The five Multi100 analysts

```{r}
#| label: tbl-five
#| tbl-cap: "The five reanalyses, with the statistic that Multi100 recorded and the conclusion of Task 1. Source: `data/analysts5.csv`."
#| echo: false
recorded_txt <- \(type, x) dplyr::case_when(
  is.na(x) ~ "none recorded",
  type == "chi2" ~ paste0("χ<sup>2</sup> = ", gsub("-", "−", formatC(x, format = "fg", digits = 5))),
  .default = paste(type, "=", gsub("-", "−", formatC(x, format = "fg", digits = 5)))
)
upper_first <- \(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))
analysts |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Analyst = id,
    Surveys = upper_first(gsub("-", "–", comparison)),
    Unit = upper_first(unit),
    Model = upper_first(outcome_model),
    `Recorded statistic` = recorded_txt(statistic_type, statistic_recorded),
    `Task 1` = task1
  ) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 5, align = "r")
```

Two analysts concluded that the data showed evidence for the claim, one that they showed evidence neither way and two that they showed evidence for the opposite. All five worked from the same file, which the SCORE replication of the paper had built from five surveys of the NSFG, and the analyses that compared the 1995 survey with a later one met a 1995 cohort that holds `r s95(2)` marriages where the paper reports 340. The [case study](index.qmd#sec-file) traces how that happened, and Task 3 asks you to find it for yourself.

---

## The tasks

The exercise runs as five numbered tasks. Each says what to do in the workspace and, where it differs, in the browser lab.

### Task 1 – The setup check

The only aim is to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. *Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE and render the report once; if it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, which prints OK when everything is in place and otherwise says what is missing. Its last check fits the reference specification of the course, which must come out at `r fmt(ref$b)` on the log scale. *Browser lab:* wait for the engine, the tables of the course and the file of the analysts to finish downloading, then run the setup cell, which reads two of the tables. If your installation will not cooperate, you can follow every later task in the browser lab, run the reproduction of Task 3 and still send both results to the class chart, but you cannot fit a specification of your own there.

### Task 2 – The data, the estimand and the graph

First, meet the data in `cohab_unions.csv` ([codebook](data/cohab_unions_codebook.md)): count the unions of each survey and the `r big(nrow(paper))` unions of the window of the paper, with their outcomes; find out how the mix of women who cohabit changed between the cohorts; turn the unions into person-months, one row for every month in which a union could end, and count the months that end in a marriage; and draw the share of each cohort that had married by each month since the couple moved in.

Second, write the **estimand statement** behind the claim. It says which unions are compared, over what time, what counts as progress to marriage, and what the comparison holds constant. The [specification menu](menu.qmd#estimand) gives the template.

Third, finish the **causal graph**. Education and race-ethnicity shape both whether a woman cohabits at all and whether a cohabiting couple marries, and cohabitation spread between the two periods, so the women who cohabited in 2005–2010 were not the same kinds of women as those of 1990–1995. Every analysis of cohabitors keeps only women who cohabited, and the graph shows what that selection does to the comparison of the two periods and which adjustment closes the paths that it opens. It also shows the difference between the two readings of the claim that the menu keeps: the change for cohabitors as they were, the change in who cohabits included, and the change within groups of the same age, race-ethnicity and education. The workspace asks dagitty, the R package for causal graphs, and draws the graph with tinyplot. dagitty cannot run in a browser tab, so the browser lab prints the answers that dagitty gives for every graph that its cell offers, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty.

### Task 3 – The reproduction

Reproduce the value that Multi100 recorded for analyst 5X3KG, **$\chi^2(1)$ = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "statistic_recorded"))` on `r big(an("5X3KG", "n_recorded"))` person-month rows**, from the file that Multi100 gave the analysts. The analyst compared the share of rows that record a marriage in the 1995 survey with that share in the 2006–2010 survey, with `prop.test()` and its continuity correction. *Workspace:* the file is in `data/` as `score_person_months.csv` ([codebook](data/score_person_months_codebook.md)), shipped unchanged, and `check_score_file()` compares its MD5 sum with that of the copy on the OSF; `prep/reproduce_5X3KG.R` holds every step of this task as a script. *Browser lab:* the page loads the same file and runs the same code, live. When the facilitator says so, the whole class types its $\chi^2$ and sends it at the same moment.

The test reproduces exactly, and it says that cohabitors became *more* likely to marry. Then find out why. Count the unions of the file one by one, from the last row of each woman, and set the 1995 cohort beside the unions of the paper: the file holds `r s95(1)` intact unions, `r s95(2)` marriages and `r s95(3)` separations, where the paper has 242, 340 and 347. Find out which of the 929 unions of the paper the file lost, and read in the codebook of the file how its 1995 rows were built. *Optional extension:* run the same test on the file with its 1995 rows rebuilt from the unions of the course, which gives $\chi^2$ = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "stat_repaired"), 2)` in the direction of the claim.

The second part of the task reproduces the result that the claim quotes. Refit Model 2 of the paper on the rebuilt unions with `fit_spec(unions, adjust = "race_period")`: a multinomial logit on person-months, weighted, with standard errors that take the strata and clusters of both surveys into account. It gives **`r fmt(model_2$b)` (SE `r fmt(model_2$se)`)** against the published −0.683 (0.14). The same model without the interaction of race-ethnicity and period, the reference specification of the course, gives `r fmt(ref$b)`. Work out what the gap between the two numbers means, by adding the interaction of each group to the period coefficient.

### Task 4 – The menu

This task is **exploratory**. `try_spec()` takes one argument per decision of the [specification menu](menu.qmd), and each defaults to the reference specification: the cohorts of the paper, every observed month, age, race-ethnicity and education held constant, weighted, the months since the start as a straight line, and a multinomial logit. Six decisions vary on the curve, `cohorts`, `horizon`, `adjust`, `weights`, `time` and `model`, so changing one thing means changing one argument. In the workspace every call is a live fit, which takes a few seconds, the multinomial logit longest; the browser lab reads the same result from the curve that the course pipeline fitted. Try several specifications, one decision at a time, and note which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. An option that is not on the curve, such as `adjust = "race_period"`, `unit = "unions"` or `comparison = "2002_2011"`, is refused with the reason given in `menu_options.csv` and the page that teaches it. `my_experiments()` prints everything that you have tried side by side. Then choose the specification that you would defend, and `submit_exploration()` sends it to the class chart on the [multiverse page](multiverse.qmd), where it appears as an open circle.

Nothing in this task is preregistered. You may look, change your mind and try again, and the chart marks the result as exploratory for that reason.

### Task 5 – Declaration and report

Choose **one** specification, one option for each of the `r n_decisions` decisions, and complete the preregistration block **before you run it**: the claim, your option for each decision, and a sentence, grounded in your causal graph, on why the specification answers the claim. `prereg()` checks the choices and prints the block with your estimand statement. `run_spec()` fits the specification that you declared, and `report_result()` sends the declared result to the class chart, where it appears as a filled circle. Then find where your result sits on the curve of `r nrow(curve)` specifications.

Task 4 and Task 5 run the same code. An exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit both so that the two sets of class results can be compared.

---

## What counts as a result

A result counts for the class chart if it is one of the `r nrow(curve)` specifications on the curve, if it reaches the chart through `submit_exploration()` or `report_result()`, which fill in the class-results form for you, and if it comes with a written reason for each choice; two sentences are enough. On this claim every specification of the curve gives a coefficient below zero that is significant at the 5% level, from `r fmt(min(curve$b))` to `r fmt(max(curve$b))`, so the class results will differ in size rather than in verdict. The reasons are what show which differences come from asking different questions, above all from the window of the later cohort and from holding the composition of cohabitors constant or not, and which from different ways of answering the same one.
